mappings.note: Asks what the paper, balloon and chalk cases have in common, i.e. whether each change can be undone, which is sorting changes by kind. Not LO-52, because the activities are recalled rather than performed and recorded.
Blow through a straw into tap water and into lime water and note what happens in each: an experiment with a control and recorded observations.
Infers the gas from the milky lime water (LO-52) and then asks whether the baking soda and water case is a physical or chemical change (LO-51). Both are put to the student.
Reports what happens to the covered and uncovered candle flames, the observation half of the demonstration. The oxygen conclusion is drawn in a separate item.

Explains how focused sunlight raises the paper to its ignition temperature so it burns without a flame being applied: a process explained step by step. Not LO-53, because the whole mechanism rather than a single cause is wanted.
Works through the burning candle, wax melting, rising up the wick and vaporising before it burns. Again a process explanation rather than a classification.
Picks the statements that hold for a physical change, including that no new substance forms. Definitional sorting of changes, so LO-51.
Judges a list of changes, from stitching cloth to soil forming from rock, for whether they can be reversed. Classification of changes throughout.
True or false on several changes, including baking soda with lemon juice and condensation of water vapour: each requires the change to be placed as physical or chemical.

Fill in the blanks across rusting, folding, combustion and burning magnesium, each ending in the physical or chemical verdict. Not LO-55, because the product name is one blank among several and no equation is required.
Water to ice and water to steam judged physical because the substance is unchanged: classification with justification.
Curdling of milk placed as a chemical change because a new substance forms and cannot be reversed.
Weathering of rock into soil judged physical because only the size of the pieces changes. Not LO-53, since the item asks for the verdict, not the mechanism of weathering.
The Prithvi story requires each step, from chopping vegetables to composting and germination, to be ticked as physical, chemical or both.
Sorts nine changes into physical only, chemical only and both, the purest classification item in the chapter.
Decides in which of four set-ups the lime water went milky and why, which is reading the results of an experiment. Not LO-51, because no change is being labelled physical or chemical.
Picks the melting ice cube as the change of state among four changes: sorting by the kind of change involved.
Chopping vegetables alters size and shape, not composition, which is what makes it physical.
Popcorn changing size, shape and texture and not turning back is the irreversible-change observation. Classification of the change, so LO-51.
Unfolding the paper boat returns the sheet, so the change was only of shape: a physical-change judgement.
Inflating and deflating a balloon placed as physical because the rubber is unchanged.
Contrasts deflating with bursting on whether the change can be undone. The contrast is between two changes, not two materials, so LO-51 rather than LO-50.
Crushed chalk is still chalk, so no new substance forms: the defining test for a physical change.
Definition of a physical change as one that alters shape, size or state only.
Changes of state judged physical because the substance stays water. Companion to the definitional item, applied to the three states.

Why exhaled air turns lime water milky while tap water does not: the effect is traced to the carbon dioxide we breathe out. Not LO-52, because the observation is given and the cause is what is wanted.
Definition of a chemical change as the formation of one or more new substances, the criterion the whole chapter sorts on.

Calcium carbonate as the product of carbon dioxide meeting lime water: a reaction product named, which is the word-equation outcome. Not LO-52, because the item asks what is formed rather than what is seen.
Milky lime water as the standard test for carbon dioxide: knowledge of a test, so the investigation outcome rather than LO-55.
Carbon dioxide named as the product of vinegar with baking soda, a reaction product.
Why that reaction counts as chemical: a new substance appears. The criterion, not the product, is what is assessed.
Baking soda fizzes with vinegar but not with water because an acid is needed: the difference in outcome traced to its cause. Not LO-51, because neither case is being labelled.
Rusting placed as a chemical change because iron oxide is a new substance.
Magnesium burning yields magnesium oxide together with heat and light: the products of the reaction.
Why burning magnesium is chemical: the new oxide, not the heat and light, is the deciding criterion. Classification, so LO-51 rather than the product item on LO-55.
Names combustion as reaction with oxygen giving out heat and light, which is the process this chapter explains. Not LO-51, because no particular change is being sorted.
Combustible substances as the class of materials that can burn. Here a class of materials, not of changes, is named, which LO-51 also covers.
What the covered-candle set-up demonstrates about oxygen: reading the conclusion off the experiment. Not LO-54, because the item points at the evidence rather than the mechanism of burning.
How to test the gas left in the tumbler, namely with lime water: a test chosen and applied.
Smothering burning clothes with a blanket cuts off oxygen, the combustion idea used in an emergency at home. Not LO-54, because the item asks why the safety measure works.
